analogy.p: Imagine a room full of set mousetraps, each with a ping-pong ball balanced on it. Throw one ball in and it springs one trap, which flings two balls into the air; they land on other traps, which fling out more balls, and within seconds every trap has gone off in a flash. That is an uncontrolled chain reaction. If you remove most of the balls or put absorbing cushions between the traps so only one new trap goes off each time, the traps fire steadily one after another, like a controlled reactor with control rods. It maps well onto neutrons triggering fissions, but it breaks down because mousetraps are reset by hand and use stored spring energy, whereas fission releases energy from the nucleus itself and the products (the fragments) are themselves radioactive.

bullets: Know the definition: **nuclear fission is the splitting of a large and unstable nucleus** (for example **uranium-235** or **plutonium-239**).
Know that **spontaneous fission is rare**, and that fission usually happens only after the unstable nucleus **absorbs a neutron**.
Know that the nucleus splits into **two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size**, and that **two or three neutrons** are released, together with **gamma rays**.
Know that **energy is released** by the reaction and that the released **neutrons may go on to start a chain reaction**.
Know that the chain reaction is **controlled in a nuclear reactor** to control the energy released.
Know that the explosion of a **nuclear weapon** is caused by an **uncontrolled chain reaction**.
Be able to **draw and interpret diagrams** showing the fission process and a chain reaction, and to balance nuclear equations for fission.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This point is in the **Physics only (triple science)** content of AQA 4.4 Atomic structure. You must be able to describe **nuclear fission**, explain how it can lead to a **chain reaction**, and say how that chain reaction is **controlled in a nuclear reactor** but **uncontrolled in a nuclear weapon**. It matters because fission supplies a large share of the world's low-carbon electricity and it is also the basis of nuclear weapons, so examiners love evaluation and explanation questions on it.

bullets: **Definition (mark-scheme style):** the **splitting of a large and unstable nucleus** into **two smaller nuclei**, with the release of **neutrons**, **gamma rays** and **energy**.
The two smaller nuclei are **roughly equal in size** (for example one with about 90 nucleons and one with about 140), not one tiny piece and one huge piece.
The fragments are themselves usually **radioactive**, because they have too many neutrons for their size.
Fission only happens with **very large nuclei** such as uranium and plutonium. Small nuclei (hydrogen, helium) do not undergo fission.
Fission is a **nuclear** process: it changes the **nucleus**. Burning coal is a **chemical** process: it only rearranges electrons.
A fission event is described by a **nuclear equation** where the total **mass number** and total **atomic number** are the same on both sides.
core.p: Fission means splitting. In **nuclear fission** a very large nucleus breaks into two smaller nuclei. This is different from radioactive decay, where a nucleus emits a small particle (alpha, beta) or gamma radiation and stays almost the same size. In fission the nucleus really does break roughly in half, which is why the daughter nuclei are called **fission fragments** or **fission products**.

bullets: **Uranium-235** has 92 protons and 143 neutrons (92 + 143 = 235). It is the main fuel in most reactors.
**Plutonium-239** has 94 protons and 145 neutrons. It is made in reactors from uranium-238 and is also used as fuel and in weapons.
**Natural uranium** is mostly uranium-238 (over 99%), which does not easily undergo fission. Only about 0.7% is uranium-235.
Reactor fuel is therefore **enriched** so that about 3 to 5% is uranium-235. Weapons need a much higher proportion. (Enrichment detail is beyond the spec but gives good context.)
The nucleus is **unstable** because of its large size: lots of **protons repel** each other and the **strong force** only just holds them together.
Do not confuse **isotopes**: uranium-235 and uranium-238 have the same number of protons (92) but different numbers of neutrons (143 and 146).
core.p: The fuels used are **uranium-235** and **plutonium-239**. Both are large nuclei with many protons packed together. The strong nuclear force that holds a nucleus together acts only over very short distances, but the **electrostatic repulsion** between protons acts across the whole nucleus. In a very large nucleus the repulsion is nearly strong enough to win, so the nucleus is only just stable and a small disturbance (absorbing a neutron) can make it split.

bullets: **Step 1:** a **neutron** travelling at a suitable speed collides with a uranium-235 nucleus and is **absorbed**.
**Step 2:** the nucleus becomes **uranium-236**, which is **very unstable** (it wobbles and stretches).
**Step 3:** the nucleus **splits into two smaller nuclei**, roughly equal in size.
**Step 4:** **two or three neutrons** and **gamma rays** are released, and the fragments fly apart with a lot of **kinetic energy**.
**Why a neutron and not a proton or alpha particle?** Neutrons are **neutral**, so they are not repelled by the positively charged nucleus. Protons and alpha particles are positive and are repelled.
Slow ('thermal') neutrons are the most likely to be absorbed by uranium-235, which is why reactors use a **moderator** to slow neutrons down (see later section).
core.h: How fission starts: absorbing a neutron
core.p: Spontaneous fission, where a nucleus splits with no outside trigger, is very rare, so it cannot be relied on to produce energy. In a reactor, fission is **induced**: a neutron strikes a uranium-235 nucleus and is **absorbed**. Neutrons have no charge, so they are not repelled by the positive nucleus and can get right in. The nucleus then holds one extra neutron, becoming a very unstable nucleus which splits.

bullets: **Example equation (plain text):** n(1,0) + U(235,92) -> Ba(141,56) + Kr(92,36) + 3 n(1,0) + energy.
**Check mass numbers:** left 1 + 235 = 236; right 141 + 92 + 3 = 236. They match.
**Check atomic numbers:** left 0 + 92 = 92; right 56 + 36 + 0 = 92. They match.
The **neutrons on the right** are the ones that can go on to cause **further fissions**.
Different fissions give different pairs of fragments (for example strontium and xenon), and **2 or 3 neutrons** each time, which is why the average is about 2.4 per fission.
If asked to find a missing number, subtract: **unknown mass number = total left - the other mass numbers on the right**, and do the same for atomic number.
**Gamma rays** are emitted as well, carrying away some of the energy. They have no mass or charge, so they do not appear in the balancing.
core.h: Products of fission and nuclear equations
core.p: A typical fission is: a neutron + uranium-235 gives two smaller nuclei + two or three neutrons + energy. The exact fragments vary from one fission to the next, but they always obey two conservation rules: **total mass number (nucleon number) is conserved** and **total atomic number (proton number) is conserved**. Check this every time you write or complete an equation.

bullets: Energy is released by the reaction: this is stored **nuclear energy** being transferred to **kinetic energy** of fragments, then to **thermal energy** of the surroundings.
A single fission of uranium-235 releases roughly **200 MeV**, millions of times more than the energy released when one carbon atom burns.
**About 1 kg of uranium-235** can release of the order of **8 x 10^13 J** if all of it undergoes fission, compared with about 3 x 10^7 J from 1 kg of coal. That is millions of times more.

**Higher-tier extension (beyond the spec wording):** the total mass of the products is **slightly less** than the mass of the starting nucleus plus neutron. This missing mass is converted to energy, as described by E = mc^2.
The energy is released as **heat** in the fuel rods, and that is what is used to make steam in a power station.
Because energy comes from the nucleus, **no carbon dioxide is released** by the fission itself.
core.h: Where does the energy come from?
core.p: The energy released in fission is huge compared with chemical reactions. Most of it appears as the **kinetic energy of the fission fragments**, which crash into neighbouring atoms and make them vibrate faster, so the fuel gets **hot**. The rest is carried by the released neutrons and the gamma rays. Because it comes from the nucleus, a tiny mass of fuel gives a vast amount of energy.

bullets: **Chain reaction:** a series of fissions in which the **neutrons released by one fission cause further fissions**.
If each fission causes **exactly one** further fission, the reaction proceeds at a **steady rate**. This is what is wanted in a **reactor**.
If each fission causes **more than one** further fission, the rate **increases exponentially**: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ... This is what happens in a **nuclear weapon**.
If each fission causes **less than one** further fission on average, the reaction **dies away** and stops.
Some neutrons **escape** from the fuel or are **absorbed by other nuclei** (such as uranium-238) without causing fission, which is why a chain reaction needs enough fuel packed closely together.
**Diagram skill:** draw a nucleus with an arrow of a neutron going in, two arrows of neutrons going out, each hitting another nucleus, branching outwards in generations.
core.p: Each fission releases two or three neutrons. If at least one of these neutrons is absorbed by another uranium-235 nucleus, that nucleus also splits, releasing more neutrons, and so on. This self-sustaining sequence is a **chain reaction**. If more than one neutron from each fission causes another fission, the number of fissions grows rapidly (it multiplies each generation), and the energy release becomes enormous in a tiny time.

bullets: **Fuel rods:** contain the uranium-235 (or plutonium-239) where fission happens and heat is produced.

**Control rods:** made of a material that **absorbs neutrons** (for example boron or cadmium). Lowering them in **absorbs more neutrons** so the reaction slows down; raising them out lets it speed up. Fully lowered rods **shut the reactor down**.
**Moderator:** a material (for example water or graphite) that **slows down the fast neutrons** so they are more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 nuclei and cause fission.
**Coolant:** a fluid (often water) that **carries the thermal energy away** from the core to a heat exchanger.
**Shielding:** thick concrete and steel around the reactor to absorb **radiation**, so workers and the public are protected.
**To control the rate:** adjust the **position of the control rods**. This is the key point for 'how is the energy released controlled?' questions.
If the reaction ever gets too fast, **emergency systems drop all control rods in** to absorb neutrons and stop the chain reaction.
core.h: Controlled chain reaction in a nuclear reactor
core.p: In a reactor the chain reaction is **controlled** so that, on average, **only one neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission**. That keeps the energy output **steady** and safe. The parts of the reactor are not all named in the AQA spec wording, but exam questions often describe them, so you should know what each does.

bullets: In a weapon, the reaction is designed to be **uncontrolled** so that a huge amount of energy is released **in a very short time**.
In a reactor, the reaction is **controlled** so that the same total energy is released **slowly and steadily** over months or years.
The **fuel** in a weapon is far more highly enriched than reactor fuel, so a reactor **cannot explode like a nuclear bomb**.
**Comparison for exam answers:** controlled = on average **one** neutron per fission causes another fission; uncontrolled = **more than one**.
The weapon releases **heat, blast and large quantities of radiation**, and leaves **radioactive fallout**.
Explain the difference using **rate of energy release** and **number of neutrons causing fission**.
core.p: The **explosion of a nuclear weapon** is caused by an **uncontrolled chain reaction**. There are no control rods or moderator to regulate it: a large mass of highly enriched fuel is brought together quickly so that, on average, **more than one** neutron from each fission goes on to cause another fission. The number of fissions doubles in a tiny fraction of a second, and the energy is released almost all at once as a violent explosion.

bullets: **Energy transfer chain:** nuclear energy -> thermal energy (in fuel and coolant) -> kinetic energy of steam -> kinetic energy of turbine -> electrical energy from generator.
A **heat exchanger** transfers energy from the hot reactor coolant to water, making steam; this keeps radioactive coolant separate from the turbine.
After the turbine the steam is **condensed** and returned to be heated again. Waste thermal energy is released at cooling towers or into the sea.
A nuclear power station is **not** 100% efficient: a lot of energy is wasted as thermal energy.
The reactor can run **continuously** and gives a **reliable base load**, unlike solar or wind which depend on weather.
Fuel is used in tiny quantities: a few kilograms of uranium can supply a power station for a long time.
core.h: From fission to electricity in a power station
core.p: A nuclear power station is essentially a very hot kettle. The fission reaction heats the coolant, which makes **steam**; the steam turns a **turbine**, which turns a **generator**. The only real difference between this and a coal or gas power station is the **source of the thermal energy**: fission of uranium instead of burning fuel.

bullets: **Advantages:** a **large amount of energy** from a **small mass of fuel**; **no carbon dioxide** during operation; **reliable** and available all the time; low running fuel costs.

**Disadvantages:** produces **radioactive waste** (fission products and contaminated materials) that must be stored safely for **thousands of years**; **very expensive** to build and to decommission; risk of **accidents** which could spread radioactive material.
**Fission products are radioactive**, many with long half-lives, which makes **waste storage** difficult. Waste is usually stored underground or in secure cooled storage.
**Public concern** is high because the risk of an accident, although tiny, has very serious consequences. This links to the idea of **perceived risk**.
The uranium mine and **enrichment** have environmental costs, and plutonium can be used for weapons, adding to security concerns.
For a 'discuss' question, always finish with a **judgement** supported by a reason, for example 'on balance...'.
core.p: Evaluation questions ask you to weigh advantages against disadvantages. Fission gives a very large, reliable amount of energy without producing carbon dioxide, but it also produces **radioactive waste** that stays dangerous for a very long time, and the consequences of an accident can be severe. Good answers give **both sides** and finish with a judgement.

bullets: **Radioactive decay:** the nucleus emits **alpha, beta or gamma** and is **random**; it cannot be speeded up or slowed down by heating.
**Fission:** the nucleus **splits in two** (usually after absorbing a neutron) and **2 or 3 neutrons** are released; it can be **controlled** with control rods.
**Fusion:** two **light nuclei join** to make a **heavier nucleus**; it needs **very high temperature and pressure**.
**Fission uses large nuclei** (uranium, plutonium); **fusion uses small nuclei** (hydrogen isotopes).
**Fission fragments** are radioactive; the main fusion product (helium) is **not** radioactive.
Both release energy because the **products are more stable** than the starting nuclei.
core.h: Fission compared with radioactive decay and with fusion
core.p: It helps to separate three nuclear changes. **Radioactive decay** (alpha, beta, gamma) is **random** and spontaneous, with a small particle emitted. **Fission** splits a big nucleus into two, usually after absorbing a neutron. **Fusion** (next spec point) joins two small nuclei into a larger one. Mixing up these terms is one of the most common ways to lose marks.

bullets: **Link to energy resources:** nuclear fuel is **non-renewable**, but it does not produce carbon dioxide, so it does not add to **climate change**.
**Link to half-life:** many fission products have long half-lives, so waste stays radioactive for a long time. A longer half-life means the activity falls more slowly.
**Link to contamination and irradiation:** a leak of radioactive material could cause **contamination**; being near a source causes **irradiation**.
**Link to isotopes:** only some isotopes (uranium-235, plutonium-239) undergo fission easily; uranium-238 does not.

**Higher-style reasoning:** if the average number of new fissions per fission is k, then k = 1 steady, k > 1 growing, k < 1 dying away. This idea is not named in the spec but is a neat way to explain control.
**Safety link:** the three ways to reduce risk from radiation are shielding, distance and short exposure time.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam-style extension
core.p: Fission appears in several other places in the course. It links to **energy resources** (non-renewable vs renewable, reliability and cost), to **atomic structure** (isotopes, nucleons, nuclear equations) and to **radiation hazards** (contamination, irradiation, half-life of waste). In extended answers you can pull these together for higher marks.

exam: **Define it (1 mark):** 'The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) into two smaller nuclei.' Always say large and unstable.
**Describe fission (2 to 3 marks):** a neutron is absorbed by the nucleus, the nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, and two or three neutrons plus energy are released.
**Chain reaction (2 to 3 marks):** the neutrons released go on to cause further fissions in other nuclei, which release more neutrons, and so on.
**Control (2 marks):** control rods absorb neutrons so that on average only one neutron from each fission causes another fission, keeping the rate steady.

**Reactor vs bomb (3 to 4 marks):** controlled chain reaction releases energy slowly and steadily; uncontrolled chain reaction, more than one neutron causes fission, so energy is released very rapidly and causes an explosion.
**Nuclear equations (2 marks):** add the mass numbers, then the atomic numbers, on each side. Show the totals. One mark for the correct number, one for working.
**Draw a diagram (3 marks):** neutron in, nucleus splits into two, 2 to 3 neutrons out, each neutron hitting another nucleus. Label nucleus, neutron and fragments.
**Evaluation (6 marks):** give at least two advantages and two disadvantages, link each to a reason, and finish with a judgement. Use words like 'however' and 'on balance'.
**Command words:** 'state' = short fact; 'describe' = what happens in order; 'explain' = what happens and why; 'evaluate' = both sides plus a judgement.
**Use the key terms:** unstable, absorbs a neutron, two smaller nuclei, chain reaction, controlled, control rods. These are the words mark schemes reward.

mistakes.r: Fission is the splitting of a large unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei. Joining is fusion.
mistakes.w: Fission is when two nuclei join together.

mistakes.r: The nucleus absorbs a neutron, which is uncharged and so is not repelled by the nucleus.
mistakes.w: Uranium splits when it is hit by a proton or an electron.

mistakes.r: Nuclear fission is not burning (combustion). It is a nuclear reaction that changes the nucleus.
mistakes.w: A nuclear reactor works by burning uranium.

mistakes.r: Control rods absorb neutrons. The moderator slows neutrons down.
mistakes.w: The control rods slow down the neutrons.

mistakes.r: It produces radioactive waste, including fission products, that must be stored safely for a very long time.
mistakes.w: A nuclear power station has no waste.

mistakes.r: A reactor has a controlled chain reaction (about one neutron per fission causes another), and its fuel is low in uranium-235; a bomb has an uncontrolled chain reaction.
mistakes.w: A nuclear reactor can explode like an atomic bomb.

mistakes.r: Fission releases two or three neutrons, which is what makes a chain reaction possible.
Total mass number and total atomic number are conserved: they must match on both sides.
mistakes.w: Writing a nuclear equation where only the mass numbers are checked, or the totals do not match.

mistakes.r: Radioactive decay is the random emission of alpha, beta or gamma; fission is the splitting of a nucleus, usually induced by a neutron.
mistakes.w: Fission is the same as radioactive decay.

summary: You must be able to describe nuclear fission as the splitting of a large unstable nucleus such as uranium-235 into two smaller nuclei with neutrons, gamma rays and energy, explain how a chain reaction forms, and contrast the controlled chain reaction in a reactor with the uncontrolled one in a weapon. It matters because fission supplies reliable low-carbon electricity but creates radioactive waste, giving plenty of explain and evaluate questions.

terms.d: The splitting of a large and unstable nucleus into two smaller nuclei, roughly equal in size, releasing neutrons, gamma rays and energy.
A large unstable isotope of uranium (92 protons, 143 neutrons) used as fuel in nuclear reactors.
A large unstable isotope (94 protons, 145 neutrons) used as nuclear fuel and in weapons.
Fission that occurs without absorbing a neutron first; it is rare.
Fission started by an unstable nucleus absorbing a neutron.
A series of fissions in which neutrons released by one fission cause further fissions.
A chain reaction in which, on average, only one neutron from each fission causes another fission, so energy is released at a steady rate (as in a nuclear reactor).
A chain reaction in which more than one neutron from each fission causes further fission, so the rate rises rapidly (as in a nuclear weapon).
The smaller nuclei formed when a nucleus undergoes fission; they are usually radioactive.
Rods that absorb neutrons, used to control the rate of fission in a reactor.
A material that slows down fast neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission.
A fluid that carries thermal energy away from the reactor core.
Rods containing the nuclear fuel in which fission takes place.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus; it is conserved in nuclear equations.
The number of protons in a nucleus; it is conserved in nuclear equations.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Waste containing radioactive nuclei, such as fission products, that must be stored safely.

worked.q: Complete the nuclear equation for fission: n(1,0) + U(235,92) -> Sr(90,38) + Xe(143,54) + x n(1,0). Find x. (2 marks)
steps: Mass numbers on right: 90 + 143 + x(1) = 233 + x.
Check atomic numbers: left 0 + 92 = 92; right 38 + 54 + 0 = 92. They match.

worked.ans: 512 fissions in generation 10; 1023 in total. This shows how quickly an uncontrolled chain reaction grows.
worked.q: A chain reaction starts with 1 fission. Each fission causes 2 further fissions in the next generation. How many fissions occur in generation 10, and how many in total from generation 1 to 10? (3 marks)
steps: Generation 1 has 1 fission, generation 2 has 2, generation 3 has 4: doubling each time.
Generation n has 2^(n - 1) fissions. For n = 10: 2^9 = 512.

worked.ans: Model answer: Each fission releases two or three neutrons. Control rods absorb neutrons so that only one neutron per fission, on average, causes another fission. This keeps the chain reaction steady and the energy release slow. They can be moved in or out to change the rate. A bomb has no such control: more than one neutron from each fission goes on to cause fission, so the number of fissions grows rapidly and releases the energy explosively.
worked.q: Explain how a chain reaction is controlled in a nuclear reactor, and why a reactor does not explode like a nuclear bomb. (4 marks)
steps: Fission of uranium-235 releases two or three neutrons which can cause further fission (chain reaction).
Control rods absorb neutrons, so on average only one neutron from each fission causes another fission.
Lowering the rods in slows the reaction; raising them speeds it up.
In a bomb the chain reaction is uncontrolled, with more than one neutron per fission causing fission, so the rate multiplies and the energy is released almost at once.
